lessons.title: Net Rental Yield: Maintenance, Property Tax, Vacancy and Brokerage

children.text: In the last lesson, the Sarjapur Road flat went from the broker's 4.0% to an honest gross yield of 3.21%. Now the owner actually lets it out. The first tenant leaves after two years, the flat sits empty for two months, the new tenant's broker wants a month's rent, BBMP sends the property tax bill, and the walls need repainting. None of that shows up in gross yield. All of it shows up in the owner's bank account. By the end of this lesson you will be able to turn any gross yield into a net yield, see which costs do the most damage, and measure what a single empty month really costs.

body.text: Gross yield is what the tenant pays. Net yield is what you keep. For a typical Indian flat, the gap between the two quietly swallows a fifth to a quarter of the rent.

children.text: The Net Yield Formula

body.latex: \text{Net Rental Yield (\%)} = \frac{\text{Annual Rent} - \text{Vacancy Loss} - \text{Owner's Operating Costs}}{\text{All-in Acquisition Cost}} \times 100
body.caption: The top line is the property's net operating income: what it earns after running costs, before income tax and loan interest.

markDefs.definition: Rent the property would earn if always occupied, minus the rent lost during empty months.
Annual rent actually collected minus the owner's running costs, before income tax and loan interest. Often shortened to NOI.

children.text: Start with the full annual rent, subtract the rent lost to empty months to get
effective rent
, then subtract every cost the owner pays to keep the flat rentable. What remains is
net operating income
. Divide it by the same all-in cost you used for gross yield, so the two numbers are directly comparable.

body.title: What net rental yield includes, and what it leaves out

columns.label: Included in net yield
points: Society maintenance you pay while the flat is empty
Brokerage to find each new tenant
Sinking fund and repair fund contributions
Rent agreement and police verification costs

columns.label: Left out, covered later
points: Home loan interest: how you financed the flat, not how the flat performs (Chapter 4)
Stamp duty and registration: already in the all-in cost, so not counted again

children.text: Sarjapur Road: From Gross to Net

markDefs.definition: A reserve that a housing society collects from owners to pay for major future repairs such as waterproofing, lift replacement or structural work.

children.text: The flat is now let at ₹32,000 a month plus maintenance, so the tenant pays the ₹4,000 monthly maintenance to the society directly. Assume tenants change every two years with a two-month gap between them, which averages one vacant month a year. The owner also pays property tax, a
sinking fund
contribution, repairs and insurance.

body.caption: Sarjapur Road 2BHK: annual net operating income (illustrative)

children.text: Net yield = ₹2,95,000 ÷ ₹1,19,61,000 × 100 = 2.47%. The flat that a broker sold as a 4% yield actually delivers under 2.5% before tax.

body.title: Where the ₹3.84 lakh of potential rent goes (₹ thousand)
Where the repair and property tax numbers come from

children.text: Repainting:
tenants usually expect a freshly painted flat. Repainting a 2BHK interior every four years at around ₹40,000 averages ₹10,000 a year.
Small repairs:
leaking taps, geyser servicing, electrical faults, broken tiles and door fittings add roughly ₹5,000 a year.
Property tax:

several municipal corporations, including those in Bengaluru and Pune, charge more property tax on a rented home than on a self-occupied one. Check your own municipal bill; do not assume the rate you paid while living there.
Special levies:
societies occasionally raise one-time charges for waterproofing, lift replacement or DG sets. These are lumpy and easy to forget, so budget for them inside the sinking fund line.

body.title: Operating cost or not?
body.question: Which of these should NOT be deducted when calculating a flat's net rental yield?
options: Brokerage paid to find a new tenant
Interest on the home loan used to buy the flat
Society maintenance paid while the flat is vacant
body.explanation: Loan interest depends on how you paid for the flat, not on how the flat performs. Two buyers of identical flats, one with cash and one with a loan, should see the same net yield. The effect of borrowing is handled separately in Chapter 4 on leverage.

children.text: Vacancy: The Cost That Does the Most Damage

An empty month hurts twice. You lose the rent, and you pay the maintenance the tenant was covering. Here is the Sarjapur Road flat's net yield at different levels of vacancy, with every other cost unchanged.

body.caption: Sarjapur Road 2BHK: how vacancy changes net yield

body.latex: \text{Yield Lost per Vacant Month} = \frac{\text{Monthly Rent} + \text{Monthly Maintenance}}{\text{All-in Acquisition Cost}} \times 100
body.caption: Sarjapur Road: (₹32,000 + ₹4,000) ÷ ₹1,19,61,000 × 100 = 0.30 percentage points.

body.label: Cost of one empty month
body.context: On a flat yielding 2.47% net, one extra vacant month a year wipes out about an eighth of the owner's net income. A reliable tenant who stays is worth more than a small rent increase.

body.text: This is why experienced landlords often accept a slightly lower rent for a stable tenant and keep annual increases modest. A ₹2,000 rent hike adds ₹24,000 a year. If it pushes a good tenant to leave and the flat sits empty for two months, the owner loses ₹72,000 in rent and maintenance plus another ₹32,000 in brokerage.

body.title: Name the leak
body.textWithBlank: Rent that a property fails to earn because it sits empty between tenants is called ___ loss.
body.explanation: Vacancy loss is the gap between potential rent and effective rent. For Indian flats, it is usually the single largest deduction between gross and net yield.

body.title: Calculate a net yield
body.prompt: A 2BHK in Velachery, Chennai cost ₹90 lakh all-in and rents for ₹25,000 a month plus maintenance. Expect one vacant month a year on average and ₹40,000 a year in total owner's operating costs. What is the net rental yield? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Potential rent = ₹25,000 × 12 = ₹3,00,000. Effective rent = ₹3,00,000 − ₹25,000 = ₹2,75,000. Net operating income = ₹2,75,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹2,35,000. Net yield = ₹2,35,000 ÷ ₹90,00,000 × 100 = 2.61%. The gross yield was 3.33%, so about 22% of the rent leaked away.

children.text: The Remote Owner Problem

Owners who live in another city or abroad face higher leakage. They cannot show the flat on a Sunday, supervise repairs or chase late rent themselves. Property management companies fill that gap, typically for a fee of a few percent of collected rent up to around 10%, and repairs arranged remotely rarely cost less.

body.title: The NRI's Gachibowli flat
body.scenario: Meera Iyer, a software architect in Singapore, owns a 2BHK in Gachibowli, Hyderabad bought for ₹1.28 crore all-in. It rents for ₹35,000 a month plus maintenance. A property manager charges 8% of rent collected. Because showings and repairs are slower from abroad, vacancy averages 1.5 months a year. Other annual costs: tenant brokerage ₹17,500 (one month's rent every two years), property tax ₹15,000, repairs ₹25,000, sinking fund ₹8,000, insurance ₹3,000, and maintenance during vacancy at ₹5,000 a month.
body.prompt: Calculate the gross yield, the net operating income and the net yield. Then suggest what Meera could do to improve the net yield.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Gross yield: ₹35,000 × 12 = ₹4,20,000. ₹4,20,000 ÷ ₹1,28,00,000 × 100 = 3.28%.
2. Vacancy loss: 1.5 × ₹35,000 = ₹52,500. Effective rent = ₹3,67,500.
3. Costs: manager fee 8% × ₹3,67,500 = ₹29,400; brokerage ₹17,500; property tax ₹15,000; repairs ₹25,000; sinking fund ₹8,000; insurance ₹3,000; maintenance while vacant 1.5 × ₹5,000 = ₹7,500. Total = ₹1,05,400.
4. Net operating income = ₹3,67,500 − ₹1,05,400 = ₹2,62,100. Net yield = ₹2,62,100 ÷ ₹1,28,00,000 × 100 = 2.05%.
5. About 38% of the potential rent leaks away, compared with 23% for the owner-managed Sarjapur Road flat.
6. Ways to improve: sign longer agreements with a lock-in period to cut turnover; ask the manager to include tenant search in the fee to avoid separate brokerage; keep rent increases modest to retain good tenants; get competing repair quotes; and compare the 2.05% honestly with what a listed REIT or a debt fund would pay with no tenant to manage.

body.title: Build your own net yield sheet
steps: Start with the signed monthly rent, excluding maintenance, and multiply by 12.
Estimate realistic vacancy from how long similar flats in your society stay empty, and subtract that rent.
Add tenant brokerage, averaged over how often tenants change.
Pull your actual property tax bill for a rented property, not a self-occupied one.
Add sinking fund, special levies, repairs, repainting and insurance, averaged per year.
Add maintenance for vacant months and any property manager fees.
Divide net operating income by all-in acquisition cost and compare it with your gross yield.

cards.definition: Annual rent minus vacancy loss and owner's operating costs, divided by all-in acquisition cost, times 100.
Potential annual rent minus rent lost during vacant months.
Effective rent minus operating costs, before income tax and loan interest.
Rent not earned while a property sits empty between tenants.
A society reserve collected from owners for major future repairs.
The share of potential rent lost to vacancy and costs. About 23% for the Sarjapur Road example.

points: Net yield = (annual rent − vacancy loss − owner's operating costs) ÷ all-in acquisition cost × 100.
Net yield excludes loan interest and income tax, so identical flats show the same net yield however they were financed.
The Sarjapur Road flat falls from 3.21% gross to 2.47% net, losing about 23% of its rent to leakage.
Vacancy is usually the biggest leak: each empty month costs about 0.3 percentage points of yield on that flat.
Keeping a good tenant is often worth more than a rent increase.
Remote owners typically face higher leakage from management fees, longer vacancies and costlier repairs.
Always check property tax at the rented-property rate, which can be higher than the self-occupied rate.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The people, properties, rents and costs shown are illustrative. Property tax rates, society charges and rental practices vary by city and change over time, so verify current figures and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making any decision.
